title: A method for evaluating the printability of concrete in 3D-printed pavement
author: Feng, Yin, et al.
materials: For 3D printed pavement concrete, different concrete mix proportion designs (e.g., amount of cement, aggregate content, etc.) can affect the printability and the quality of the pavement concrete. Therefore, indoor experiments were conducted using a developed mini-3D printing paver to investigate the impact of mix proportion designs on the printability of 3D-printed pavement concrete in this study. The water-cement ratios (w/c) of the three mix proportions were 0.35, 0.40, and 0.45, respectively. The main gel material utilized in the work was P.O 42.5 ordinary Portland cement manufactured by Shanshui Cement Group in Shandong Province, China. Its properties were in accordance with the requirements of Chinese standard GB175–2007. In addition, low-calcium fly ash with a density of 2230 kg/m3 from Shandong Province, China, was incorporated as a mineral admixture with the objective of reducing the amount of cement, increasing the fluidity of the concrete mix and improving workability. steps.title: Assemble and prepare mini‑3D paver
steps.instruction: Construct the mini‑3D printing paver according to the design: overall dimensions length 650 mm, width 500 mm, height 450 mm; include top plate, baffle plate, finishing plate, loading table, pushing plate, locating plate, transition plate and pulleys. The box is plexiglass with an opening at top and bottom, closed front end and rear printing outlet. Install pulleys on both sides of the bottom so they can run on the track fixed on the printing platform. Bond the loading table, vertical baffle plate, inclined plate and horizontal plate with strong glue and secure them with bolts on the side walls. Drill holes at different heights on the side walls to allow angle and height adjustment of these components and fasten with bolts. Attach transition plates at the rear sides of the box. Ensure the paver width is 50–100 mm smaller than the track width. Coat the bottom plate and the tracks with lubricant before use.

steps.title: Prepare concrete mixes according to Table 4
steps.instruction: Prepare three concrete mix designs with water‑cement ratios (w/c) of 0.35, 0.40 and 0.45. Use P.O 42.5 ordinary Portland cement (Shanshui Cement Group, GB175‑2007). Use low‑calcium fly ash (density 2230 kg/m³) as mineral admixture. Use river sand (fineness modulus 2.79) as fine aggregate and continuously graded gravel (5 mm–25 mm) as coarse aggregate. The mix proportions (kg/m³) are given in Table 4 as the following raw strings: 0.3534014675396117, 0.403281408498651870, 0.45312134945769201. Adjust water content to achieve the specified w/c ratios.

steps.title: Load concrete and print slab specimen
steps.instruction: Pour the freshly mixed concrete into the loading table of the paver. Fill the space delimited by the V‑shaped top plate, bottom plate, vertical baffle plate, front wall of the box, side walls and inclined plate until the space is completely occupied. Activate the powered traction system and drive the paver at a uniform speed of 2.0–2.5 cm/s while continuously supplying concrete from the loading table. Keep the concrete level in the vertical baffle plate constant so that the concrete on the bottom plate experiences continuous, uniform pressure. Continue until the concrete has fully slid off the loading table and been extruded through the inclined plate, then pull the paver off the bottom plate without disturbing the extruded concrete. Ensure the total elapsed time from mixing to completion of paving does not exceed 20 min.

steps.title: Perform edge slump test
steps.instruction: Using the mini‑3D printing paver, print a slab‑shaped concrete specimen approximately 50 cm long. Immediately after printing, measure the slab thickness (h) at the initial printed state. After 15 min, measure the horizontal distance (Δd₁₅ₘᵢₙ) between the slump position of the slab edge and its initial position at three different locations on the same specimen. Compute the relative edge slump δ (%) for each location using δ = (Δd₁₅ₘᵢₙ / h) × 100. Take the mean of the three δ values as the final edge‑slump result.

steps.title: Conduct shape‑holding strength test
steps.instruction: Cast the concrete mixture into a bottomless cylindrical mold (diameter 15 cm, height 20 cm) without any additional consolidation. After the concrete sets, lift the mold vertically and inspect the specimen within 1 min; if there is no deformation or only minimal deformation, the specimen has good shape‑holding ability. For the strength measurement, place a second cylinder of the same dimensions (15 cm × 20 cm) on top of the specimen. Continuously and uniformly pour fine sand into the upper cylinder at a rate of 50 g s⁻¹ until the concrete specimen collapses. Record the mass of sand (m, in kg) at collapse. Calculate the shape‑holding strength σ (kPa) using σ = m · g / (π r²), where g = 9.8 m s⁻² and r = 0.075 m (radius of the cylinder). Repeat the entire procedure for three specimens of the same mix and use the average σ as the final result.

steps.title: Assess surface smoothness via image analysis
steps.instruction: Capture a photograph of the printed concrete surface with a calibrated camera that provides horizontal alignment and uniform illumination. Crop each image to a square of side length 50 cm to standardize the analysis area. In MATLAB, binarize the image using a gray‑level threshold of 127: pixel values 0–127 are set to 0 (black, representing voids) and 128–255 are set to 1 (white, representing compact areas). Compute the total void area A₁ (cm²) and the total selected area A₀ (cm²). Calculate the pore‑area percentage p (%) as p = (A₁ / A₀) × 100. Perform this analysis for each specimen.

steps.title: Score and evaluate overall printability
steps.instruction: For each concrete mix, assign points to the three test results: excellent = 3, good = 2, average = 1, poor = 0. Sum the points. If the total score ≥ 8, the mix has excellent printability. If the total score is ≥ 6 and < 8 and at least one single property scores ≥ 2, the mix has good printability. Otherwise, the mix does not meet the printability requirements and should be reformulated and re‑tested.

description: This evaluation method does not seem to be suitable for concrete with high fluidity, such as self-compacting concrete. For assessing the printability of such materials, future work must incorporate dynamic rheological tests (e.g., l-box, V-funnel) coupled with quantitative analysis of shear-thinning behavior, which will be the focus of our follow-up research.
